title: Repetitions
statement_md: You are given a DNA string of characters A, C, G, and T. Find the longest repetition — the maximum length of a contiguous substring consisting of a single character.

key_insights: Track current run length while scanning
Reset when the character changes
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Walk the string once, maintaining the streak of equal characters. Update the answer whenever the streak grows.

title: Increasing Array
statement_md: You are given an array of $n$ integers. In one move you may increase any element by one. What is the minimum number of moves to make the array non-decreasing?

key_insights: Never decrease earlier elements
Each $a_i$ must become at least $\max(a_1..a_{i-1})$
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Scan left to right. Keep the running maximum so far. If $a_i$ is smaller, add $\textit{max}-a_i$ moves and leave the max unchanged; otherwise update the max.

title: Bit Strings
statement_md: Your task is to calculate the number of bit strings of length $n$. Since the answer can be very large, print it modulo $10^9+7$.

key_insights: Answer is $2^n \bmod (10^9+7)$
Use iterative multiply or binary exponentiation
approaches.editorial_summary_md: There are $2^n$ binary strings. Compute the power modulo $10^9+7$ with a loop or fast pow.

title: Distinct Numbers
statement_md: You are given a list of $n$ integers. Your task is to calculate the number of distinct values in the list.

key_insights: Sort then count runs of equal values
A set / unordered set also works
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Sort the array and count how many times consecutive values differ, or insert into a set and take its size.

title: Movie Festival
statement_md: In a movie festival, $n$ movies will be shown. You know the starting and ending time of each movie. What is the maximum number of movies you can watch entirely? You can watch a movie only if its start is $\ge$ the previous movie's end.

key_insights: Sort by end time instead of start time
Always take the next movie that finishes earliest among feasible ones
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Classic activity selection: sort intervals by ending time and greedily pick the next compatible movie.

title: Restaurant Customers
statement_md: You are given the arrival and leaving times of $n$ customers in a restaurant. What was the maximum number of customers simultaneously present?

key_insights: Turn each customer into +1 at arrival and -1 at departure
Process events in time order; track running sum
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Create $2n$ events (arrive / leave), sort by time (leave before arrive on ties if needed), and scan while maintaining the current occupancy.

title: Dice Combinations
statement_md: Your task is to count the number of ways to construct sum $n$ by throwing a dice one or more times. Each throw gives an integer between $1$ and $6$. Order matters. Print the answer modulo $10^9+7$.

key_insights: Order of throws matters so this is permutations, not combinations
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Let $dp[x]$ be ways to form sum $x$. Transition by the last face. Base $dp[0]=1$. Compute up to $n$ modulo $10^9+7$.

title: Minimizing Coins
statement_md: Consider a money system with $n$ coins of values $c_1,\dots,c_n$. You want to form sum $x$ using as few coins as possible. Print the minimum number of coins, or $-1$ if impossible.

key_insights: $dp[s] = \min_c (dp[s-c]+1)$
Initialize unreachable states with a large sentinel
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Classic unbounded knapsack for coin change (min coins). Fill a 1D array of size $x+1$ updating with each coin value.

title: Coin Combinations II
statement_md: Consider a money system with $n$ coins. Count the number of ordered-by-coin-type combinations that produce sum $x$ (order of coins does not create new combinations). Print modulo $10^9+7$.

key_insights: Loop coins outside sums to count combinations (not permutations)
Contrast with Coin Combinations I where order matters
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Use unbounded knapsack with the coin loop outside the sum loop so each multiset is counted once.

title: Book Shop
statement_md: You have $n$ books. The $i$-th book costs $h_i$ and has $s_i$ pages. You can buy each book at most once and have budget $x$. Maximize the total number of pages.

key_insights: Each book is taken at most once → 0/1 knapsack
Iterate weights backwards to save space
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Standard 0/1 knapsack with capacity $x$, value = pages, weight = price. Use a rolling 1D DP updating from high capacity to low.

title: Removing Digits
statement_md: You are given an integer $n$. On each step you may subtract one of the digits of the current number. How many steps are needed to go from $n$ down to $0$?

key_insights: $dp[x] = 1 + \min_{\text{digit } d \text{ of } x} dp[x-d]$
Greedy always subtract largest digit is not always optimal to prove casually — DP is safe
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Compute $dp[0..n]$ bottom-up. For each $x$, try subtracting each digit appearing in the decimal representation of $x$.

title: Grid Paths
statement_md: Consider an $n \times n$ grid with some trapped squares `*`. Count paths from the top-left to the bottom-right moving only right or down, avoiding traps. Print modulo $10^9+7$.

key_insights: $dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]$ if free
Trapped cells contribute $0$
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Standard path-counting DP on a grid with blocked cells. Initialize start to $1$ if free.

title: Message Route
statement_md: Syrjälä's network has $n$ computers and $m$ connections. What is the minimum number of computers on a route from computer $1$ to computer $n$? Also reconstruct one such route.

key_insights: Unweighted shortest path → BFS
Store parent[v] to reconstruct the path
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Run BFS from $1$. If $n$ is reached, walk parents back to $1$ and reverse the path. Otherwise print IMPOSSIBLE.

title: Labyrinth
statement_md: You are given a map of a labyrinth with walls `#`, floor `.`, start `A`, and end `B`. Find the shortest path from A to B moving up/down/left/right, and print the sequence of moves.

key_insights: Treat the grid as an unweighted graph
Store previous move / parent cell for reconstruction
approaches.editorial_summary_md: BFS from A on the grid graph. Keep a parent direction for each cell and reconstruct the path when B is found.

title: Round Trip
statement_md: Given an undirected graph, find any cycle of length at least $4$ (a path that starts and ends at the same city and visits at least two other cities). Print the cycle or IMPOSSIBLE.

key_insights: On finding a back edge to a non-parent ancestor, a cycle exists
Reconstruct using the recursion stack / parent array
approaches.editorial_summary_md: DFS the undirected graph. When you see an edge to an already-visited non-parent node, recover the cycle along parents.

title: Tree Diameter
statement_md: You are given a tree of $n$ nodes. Find the diameter: the maximum number of edges on any path.

key_insights: Diameter endpoints: farthest from an arbitrary node, then farthest from that
Works specifically because the graph is a tree
approaches.editorial_summary_md: From any node find the farthest node $u$. From $u$ find the farthest node $v$. Distance $u$–$v$ is the diameter.

title: Shortest Routes II
statement_md: There are $n$ cities and $m$ flights with lengths. Process $q$ queries asking for the shortest distance between two cities (or $-1$ if unreachable).

key_insights: n ≤ 500 ⇒ all-pairs Floyd fits
Take min over parallel edges before FW
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Build an adjacency matrix with edge minima, run Floyd-Warshall, then answer each query in $O(1)$.

title: High Score
statement_md: A game has $n$ rooms and $m$ tunnels. Each tunnel gives a score. Starting in room $1$, what is the maximum score you can achieve when reaching room $n$? If the score can be arbitrarily large, print $-1$.

key_insights: Negate scores and find shortest path, or run BF for longest path
A positive cycle reachable from 1 that can reach n ⇒ answer -1
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Use Bellman-Ford for longest paths (or negate edges for shortest). After $n-1$ relaxations, one more pass detects improving cycles; check reachability into $n$.

title: Frog 1
statement_md: There are $N$ stones in a row. The height of stone $i$ is $h_i$. A frog starts on stone $1$ and wants stone $N$. From stone $i$ it may jump to $i+1$ or $i+2$, paying $|h_i - h_j|$. Find the minimum total cost.

key_insights: Classic intro DP transition
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Define $dp[i]$ as min cost to reach stone $i$. Transition from the previous one or two stones.

title: Knapsack 1
statement_md: There are $N$ items with weight $w_i$ and value $v_i$. Choose a subset with total weight $\le W$ maximizing total value. Each item at most once.

key_insights: State is (item index, remaining capacity) or rolling 1D weight
Iterate weights backwards to save space
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Standard 0/1 knapsack. $dp[w] = \max(dp[w], dp[w-w_i]+v_i)$ processed per item from high $w$ to low.

title: Watermelon
statement_md: Pete and Billy want to divide a watermelon of weight $w$ into two parts with even positive weights. Print YES or NO.

key_insights: Need $w \ge 4$ and $w$ even
2 cannot be split into two positive even parts
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Any even $w \ge 4$ works (e.g. $2+(w-2)$). Odd weights and $w=2$ fail.

title: Theatre Square
statement_md: Theatre Square is an $n \times m$ rectangle. Flagstones are $a \times a$. How many flagstones are needed to pave the square? Flagstones may extend past the border and cannot be broken.

key_insights: Answer is $\lceil n/a \rceil \cdot \lceil m/a \rceil$
Use 64-bit integers for large products
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Tiles along each side use ceiling division. Multiply the two counts with 64-bit arithmetic.

title: Books
statement_md: You have $n$ books in a row; book $i$ takes $a_i$ minutes. You have $t$ free minutes and must read a contiguous segment. What is the maximum number of books you can finish?

key_insights: Maintain a window with sum $\le t$
Expand right, shrink left when sum exceeds $t$
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Sliding window over the contiguous segment. Advance the right endpoint and move left until the sum fits in $t$; track max length.

title: Fence Painting
statement_md: Farmer John paints the interval $[a,b)$ on a fence; Bessie paints $[c,d)$. How many units of fence are painted at least once?

key_insights: Length $= (b-a)+(d-c) - \text{overlap}$
Overlap is $\max(0, \min(b,d)-\max(a,c))$
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Compute each painter's length and subtract the intersection of the two half-open intervals.

title: Towers
statement_md: You are given $n$ cubes in order. Process them one by one: place each cube on top of a tower so that it sits on a strictly larger cube, or start a new tower. What is the minimum number of towers?

key_insights: Always place on the tower with the smallest top that is still $> cube$
Equivalent to length of longest non-decreasing subsequence intuition
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Maintain the sorted tops of towers in a multiset. For each cube, upper_bound the first top strictly greater and replace it; else create a new tower.

title: String Matching
statement_md: Given a string $s$ and a pattern $p$, count how many times $p$ occurs in $s$ as a contiguous substring.

key_insights: Build the prefix-function (pi) of $p + \# + s$
Count positions where $\pi[i] = |p|$
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Use KMP: concatenate pattern, separator, and text; every place the prefix function equals $|p|$ is an occurrence. Z-algorithm works similarly.

title: Word Combinations
statement_md: You are given a string $s$ of length $n$ and a dictionary of $k$ words. Count the number of ways to form $s$ by concatenating dictionary words. Print modulo $10^9+7$.

key_insights: $dp[i]$ = ways to form prefix $s[0..i)$
From each $i$, walk a trie of dictionary words over $s[i..]$
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Insert all dictionary words into a trie. Let $dp[0]=1$. For each position, traverse the trie along the suffix and add $dp[i]$ into reachable ends.

title: Array Division
statement_md: You are given an array of $n$ positive integers. Divide it into $k$ contiguous subarrays so that the maximum subarray sum is minimized. What is that minimum possible maximum?

key_insights: Monotone predicate: can we split into $\le k$ parts with max sum $\le mid$?
Greedy scan adds a new part whenever sum would exceed mid
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Binary search the maximum allowed sum. Feasibility is a left-to-right greedy that opens a new subarray whenever adding the next element would exceed the candidate.

title: Tasks and Deadlines
statement_md: You have $n$ tasks. Task $i$ takes $a_i$ time units and has deadline $d_i$. You start at time $0$ and do tasks sequentially. Reward for finishing a task at time $f$ is $d_i - f$. Maximize the total reward.

key_insights: Optimal order is increasing duration $a_i$ (independent of deadlines)
Total reward $= \sum d_i - \sum$ finish times under that order
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Sort tasks by increasing processing time and simulate. Deadlines only affect the constant $\sum d_i$; finish times are minimized by shortest-job-first.

title: Subarray Sums I
statement_md: Given an array of $n$ positive integers, count the number of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals $x$.

key_insights: All $a_i > 0$ ⇒ window sum is monotone as right advances
Advance left while sum $> x$
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Maintain a sliding window. Expand right; shrink left while the sum exceeds $x$; count when sum equals $x$.

title: Subarray Sums II
statement_md: Given an array of $n$ integers (possibly negative), count contiguous subarrays whose sum equals $x$.

key_insights: Subarray $(l,r]$ has sum $x$ iff $\textit{pref}[r]-\textit{pref}[l]=x$
Count previous prefixes equal to $\textit{pref}[r]-x$
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Scan prefix sums left to right. Before adding the current prefix, query how many earlier prefixes equal $\textit{pref}-x$, then insert $\textit{pref}$ into the map (include $0$ initially).

title: Company Queries I
statement_md: A company has a tree hierarchy rooted at employee $1$. You process $q$ queries: given employee $x$ and integer $k$, who is the $k$-th boss above $x$? Print $-1$ if none.

key_insights: Precompute $up[v][j]$ = $2^j$-th ancestor of $v$
Answer each query by walking bits of $k$
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Build the parent tree, then binary-lifting table. For query $(x,k)$, jump according to set bits of $k$; if you fall off the root, answer $-1$.

title: Distance Queries
statement_md: You are given a tree of $n$ nodes. Process $q$ queries asking for the distance (number of edges) between two nodes.

key_insights: $\mathrm{dist}(a,b) = \mathrm{depth}[a]+\mathrm{depth}[b]-2\cdot\mathrm{depth}[\mathrm{lca}(a,b)]$
Binary lifting answers LCA in $O(\log N)$
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Root the tree, store depths, preprocess LCA with binary lifting, then answer each distance query with the depth formula.

title: Range Sum Queries I
statement_md: Given an array of $n$ integers, process $q$ queries. Each query asks for the sum of values in range $[a,b]$ (1-indexed).

key_insights: Static range sum ⇒ prefix array
Answer is $\textit{pref}[b]-\textit{pref}[a-1]$
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Build prefix sums once in $O(n)$, then each query is $O(1)$. No Fenwick/segment tree needed because there are no updates.

title: Range Update Queries
statement_md: You have an array of $n$ integers and $q$ operations: either increase every value in range $[a,b]$ by $u$, or print the value at position $k$.

key_insights: Range add + point query ⇒ Fenwick on a difference array
Add $+u$ at $a$, $-u$ at $b+1$; query is prefix sum to $k$
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Maintain a Fenwick tree of difference values. Range updates become two point updates; a point query is a prefix sum.

title: Treasure Hunting
statement_md: You are on an $n \times m$ grid. Some cells contain treasures. You may only move right, left, or up, and you can only change rows using special safe columns. Collect all treasures with minimum moves (starting at $(1,1)$).

key_insights: Process treasure rows bottom-up / top-down keeping only leftmost and rightmost per row
Transitions jump via nearest safe columns when changing rows
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Compress to rows that contain treasures. DP states track ending at the leftmost or rightmost treasure of the current row; moving to the next treasure row uses the closest safe columns for vertical travel.

title: Frog 2
statement_md: Same as Frog 1, but from stone $i$ the frog may jump to any of $i+1,\dots,i+K$ (within bounds), paying $|h_i-h_j|$. Minimize cost to reach stone $N$.

key_insights: $dp[i] = \min_{1 \le j \le K} dp[i-j] + |h_i-h_{i-j}|$
Generalizes Frog 1 ($K=2$)
approaches.editorial_summary_md: For each stone, try all jumps of length $1..K$ from earlier stones. $O(NK)$ is fine under the constraints.

title: How Many Trees?
statement_md:
Count the number of different **labeled** binary trees that can be built using exactly $n$ distinct elements.

With one element $A$, there is one tree. With two elements $A$ and $B$, there are four trees:

[[figure:binary-trees]]

Given several $n$ ($1 \le n \le 300$), print the count for each. Input ends with $0$.

```text
Sample input:
1
2
10
0

Sample output:
1
4
60949324800
```

key_insights: Unlabeled binary tree shapes are Catalan numbers $C_{n}$
Labeled count is $C_n \cdot n!$ (assign labels to nodes)
Need big integers for $n$ up to 300
approaches.editorial_summary_md: The number of labeled binary trees on $n$ nodes is $n! \cdot C_n$ where $C_n$ is the $n$-th Catalan number. Precompute with big-integer DP.

title: Euclidiana
statement_md:
A strange map numbers cells in a **counter-clockwise spiral** starting at $0$ in the center (Cartesian origin). Cell centers are at integer coordinates with unit spacing.

[[figure:spiral-grid]]

You may also think of the same pattern as a monospace matrix:

```grid
.  .  . 15  .  .  .
.  . 14  6 16  .  .
. 13  5  1  7 17  .
24 12  4  0  2  8 18
. 23 11  3  9 19  .
.  . 22 10 20  .  .
.  .  . 21  .  .  .
```

Given many pairs of cell ids $A,B$ ($0 \le A,B \le 10^9$), print the Euclidean distance between their centers. Terminate on $-1\ -1$.

key_insights: Find the ring $r$ containing id $k$ from ring lengths $8r$
Walk the ring perimeter to recover $(x,y)$
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Invert the spiral: locate the ring of each id, then the offset along that ring, yielding integer coordinates. Output Euclidean distance (typically printed with fixed precision).

title: Maja
statement_md:
Bees live on a hexagonal hive. **Maja** uses axial coordinates $(x,y)$. **Willi** numbers cells in a clockwise spiral starting at $1$ in the center.

![Hex hive coordinate systems](asset:hex-hive)

For each Willi number ($< 10^5$), print Maja's coordinates.

Sample: $1 \mapsto (0,0)$, $2 \mapsto (0,1)$, $3 \mapsto (-1,1)$, $4 \mapsto (-1,0)$, $5 \mapsto (0,-1)$.

key_insights: Hex grid has 6 directions; ring $r$ has $6r$ cells
Simulate spiral from center or closed-form ring + offset
Match the sample orientation carefully (clockwise vs CCW)
approaches.editorial_summary_md: Find which ring contains Willi's id, then walk the six sides of that hex ring to recover axial $(x,y)$.
